title: File names in scripts
summary: Names can hold spaces, line breaks and leading dashes, and a pattern can match nothing: scripts handle all of it.

scheme: for f in $(ls); do      ✘ cut at spaces
for f in ./*; do        ✔ each name whole
text: The shell expands ./* into the names themselves: one word each, even with spaces or line breaks inside.
- ✘ $(ls) gives text instead, and the shell cuts that text at every space and line break.
- [[ -f $f ]] || continue skips what isn't a regular file, like folders.
A file name can start with a dash. Handed to a command, it looks like an option.
- -- ends the options: whatever follows is a name.
- Or start the pattern with ./ : every name then starts with ./, never with a dash.

scheme: for f in ./*.jpg; do   turns once,
shopt -s nullglob      ✔ no match: no turn
text: When nothing matches, bash keeps the pattern as it is (zsh stops with an error instead). The loop then turns once, on a name that doesn't exist.
- shopt -s nullglob turns 'no match' into an empty list.
- Or test inside the loop: [[ -e $f ]] || continue.
For a whole tree, let find hand the names over safely:
- -exec cmd {} + runs cmd on many names at once, each one whole.
- -print0 ends each name with a zero byte, the one character a name can't hold: xargs -0 and read -d '' cut there, and only there.
- IFS= keeps the spaces at both ends of a line, -r keeps its backslashes.
- Every command inside the loop shares the loop's input. ssh reads it to pass it on, and swallows the rest of the list: give it -n, or < /dev/null.
- ✘ for line in $(cat file) cuts at every space, not only at line ends.
